title: Noach: the window (Genesis 6:16)
hook: the ark had a tzohar for light; midrash says it was a glowing stone

segments.voice: Yesterday, tamim: Noah was whole-hearted, undivided, in a world coming apart. Your line was whole-hearted. What did you do with all of you? Day one hundred sixty-seven.

Forget the picture-book ark with a giraffe's head poking out the top. The Torah's ark is something else: a huge wooden box, sealed with pitch inside and out, three decks, crowded with animals, and Noah's family. The rain falls for forty days. The door is shut; the text says God shut it. Then the waiting, month after month as the text counts them, inside. How does anyone live in a closed box that long? The blueprint God gives Noah is very short, only a few verses. But one line in it is about light. Today's word is the thing that let it in.
screen: `A HUGE SEALED WOODEN BOX.` → `THE DOOR IS SHUT, MONTH AFTER MONTH.` → `ONE LINE ABOUT LIGHT.`

segments.voice: God tells Noah to make a tzohar for the ark, and finish it a cubit from the top. What's a tzohar? It's a rare word, and nobody is completely sure. Some readers hear in it tzohorayim, noon, the brightest part of the day, so something to do with light. The rabbis in the midrash offer two answers, and Rashi repeats both. One teacher says it was a window, an opening near the roof. Another says it was a precious stone, a gem that glowed and lit the ark from within. A window lets light in from outside. A glowing stone makes light inside, even when outside is dark. Each says something different. The window says: even in a flood, keep one opening to the world. Don't seal yourself in completely. The stone says: when there's no light outside at all, carry some within. Much later, Hasidic teachers played with a different word in the same verse. The Hebrew for ark, teivah, also means a word. So when God tells Noah to come into the teivah, they heard: come into the word. Step inside the words of your prayer, or your study, and make them a place of shelter, with a light in them. And some readers notice what the plan leaves out. It mentions no rudder, no oars, no sail. Noah, as the text tells it, doesn't steer. What he could do was make sure there was light inside.
screen: `TZOHAR: A RARE WORD FOR LIGHT.` · `A WINDOW, OR A GLOWING STONE.` · `TEIVAH: AN ARK, AND A WORD.` · `NO RUDDER, BUT LIGHT INSIDE.` · then, large: `MAKE A WINDOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your window and your stone. Settle, and breathe. Think of something that feels like a flood right now, a worry, a hard stretch. Where's one window: one opening to the world outside it, one person, one place you can look out? Then find a stone: one small light you carry inside, a memory, a word, a reason. Rest your attention on it, and let it glow. The bell holds the time.
Tzohar. The ark's source of light, a rare word: a window, some say, and some say a glowing stone.
Your line: make a window. Today, open the curtains in a dark room, or reach out to someone who's been shut in. Day one hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: Jewish readers study the tzohar with Rashi and the midrash, and Hasidic teachers use the double meaning of teivah, ark and word, to teach about entering the words of prayer.

fork.setup: you're Noah. the door has been shut, the rain is falling, and it's dark inside the ark. what did God tell you to build for this?
options: a rudder to steer out of the storm.
fork.reveal: a tzohar. the rabbis say a window, or a glowing stone. either way: light inside when you can't steer.

original.note: Hebrew: a source of light for the ark; some connect it to tzohorayim, noon.

trapdoor: what you thought: the ark had a window, like a house.
what it means: the ark had a tzohar, a rare word; the rabbis say a window or a glowing gem.
what a scholar hears: a rare word whose sense is debated; Genesis Rabbah 31:11 (Rabbi Abba bar Kahana: a window; Rabbi Levi: a precious stone); the Baal Shem Tov's reading of teivah as 'word'.

sources.ref: Baal Shem Tov on teivah (Keter Shem Tov / Tzava'at HaRivash)

notes: Genesis 6:16 is paraphrased, not quoted (JPS 1917 reads 'A light shalt thou make to the ark' per the writer's memory; not certain).
Tzohar as a hapax in the Torah (the word in the sense of 'light/window' appears only here): confirm.
Genesis Rabbah 31:11: which teacher says window, which says gem. Script leaves them unnamed.
The Hasidic 'come into the teivah / word' teaching is usually attributed to the Baal Shem Tov (Tzava'at HaRivash 75 / Keter Shem Tov); confirm citation.
'God shut the door' (Genesis 7:16) and 'a year' inside (7:11 to 8:14): confirm.
'No rudder, no oars, no sail': the Torah gives no such details; framed as 'people notice'.
